source_description: Arthur O. Lovejoy manuscript notebook; notes on future life, death, eschatology, ritual, social and moral determinants.

batch.method: Manual visual correction against rendered PDF pages, using PaddleOCR-VL output only as a scaffold.
policy: Preserve Lovejoy’s conceptual distinctions and abbreviations where readable.
Do not silently normalize uncertain ethnographic proper names or bibliography.
Mark uncertain readings explicitly rather than reconstructing from outside knowledge.
Inserted slips are recorded as part of the PDF page on which they appear.
batch.status: first pass complete; direct-original second-pass wording propagated for pp.16, 18, 19 and inserted Marillier material on pp.29–30

research_signals_from_batch: Distinction between naturalistic, ritual/social, and strictly moral determinants of afterlife destiny
Suicide as initially a clan-solidarity/taboo category rather than intrinsically moral guilt

PDF p.18 directly reasons that killing another or oneself strikes at the clan as a whole through one of its members; the suicide's separate post-mortem village is therefore social/exclusionary evidence rather than automatically moral judgment.
Missionary/contact influence as a source-critical problem in ethnographic evidence

PDF p.19 directly calls early-nineteenth-century Western-tribe testimony 'profoundly suspect' because of extensive and partly unconscious intermingling of missionary influence; provenance/chronology is therefore part of Lovejoy's evidential test, not later editorial caution.
Universal happy afterlife as naturalistic continuation rather than reward
Emergence of moral eschatology through differentiation of destinations, judgment, and preliminary places of trial
Physical/corporeal continuity of soul and second-death/limited-afterlife conceptions
Comparative ethnographic notes on Pawnee, Cheyenne, Australian, Madagascar/Hova materials

PDF pp.29–30 are physically inserted Marillier survivance sheets: p.29 explicitly distinguishes three populations/layers in Madagascar, including the Hovas of the plateau as more Asian than African in origin; p.30 separately records non-Hova terminology, Hova-country geography, occupations of the dead, corporeal-double ideas, second death, and limited future life.

pages.corrected_text: Continuation of comparative stages in future-life beliefs. Lovejoy treats a similar intermediate form among many peoples as lying between supernatural/ritual and moral determination. The right-hand page cites a travel/narrative source on Dakota life and says its account gives a curious mingling of indigenous ideas and borrowed notions; missionary intercourse therefore has to be considered when separating later elements from more primitive ones.

pages.corrected_text: Discussion of suicide and other forms of death. Lovejoy asks whether apparent moral change may arise through natural evolution of ideas or missionary influence. In the example, most go to a better world except those violating custom or committing suicide. He stresses that violation of custom/taboo or ritual interdict is not itself equivalent to violation of a moral order.
uncertain_readings: Proper names and abbreviated ethnographic/bibliographic references retained conservatively where handwriting is unclear.

pages.corrected_text: Reason for placing suicide among deaths leading to a distinct/punitive fate is not necessarily moral. Lovejoy tests a clan-solidarity explanation: whether a man murders another or himself, 'in any case one strikes equally at [the] clan as a whole in striking at one of its members.' Murder is commonly punished by exclusion/banishment from social and religious rights and connections. The suicide is already outside the clan; the afterlife analogue is similarly social-spatial: suicides live together in a separate village away from the others, 'a village for themselves.'
pages.transcription_confidence: high for the clan-strike and separate-village argument; medium-high overall
uncertain_readings: A few connecting clauses about the punishment of murder are compressed.
Articles supplied editorially in the quoted-summary syntax.
pages.text_layer: direct-image key wording plus conservative summary
pages.witness_status: W3 for clan-as-whole reasoning and separate-village conclusion
pages.editorial_argument_summary: The page offers a social/group-jurisdiction mechanism for suicide's distinct fate; it should not be normalized into moral guilt without further evidence.

pages.corrected_text: In later periods, under the influence of moral conceptions infiltrating from a higher stage of culture or through contact, suicide may be reclassified into a place where special punishment is undergone. A travel account on North-American / western tribal future-life belief is then treated source-critically. Lovejoy writes that already in 1819 such statements were 'profoundly suspect' on account of an 'extensive' and partly 'unconscious intermingling' of missionary influence. He therefore treats chronology and contact history as necessary controls before accepting apparently moralized eschatology as indigenous evidence.
pages.transcription_confidence: high for 'profoundly suspect' / missionary-intermingling argument; medium for source title/name
uncertain_readings: Exact author/title and one tribal/locality reference remain difficult.
One qualifier before 'intermingling of missionary influence' is compressed but the evidential caution is clear.

pages.witness_status: W3 for source-critical suspicion and missionary-influence mechanism
pages.editorial_argument_summary: This is direct manuscript evidence that Lovejoy is already doing provenance/contact criticism of ethnographic testimony, not merely comparing reported beliefs at face value.

pages.corrected_text: Methodological note on introduction of the moral/social element into eschatology by diffusion of ideas from more developed peoples. Half-moral character of the notion: manner in which a corpse enters the future world is determined by its evil action or by ritual/manual causes; the afterlife does not become moral until fate/punishment/reward depends on desert. Right page: future-life idea still shows physical character. References include Radcliffe-Brown, Howitt, and other Australian material; spirit-animals and walking/dead-body conceptions are treated as bodily or quasi-physical continuities.
uncertain_readings: Proper names and abbreviated ethnographic/bibliographic references retained conservatively where handwriting is unclear.

pages.corrected_text: Setting-sun / primitive-unity discussion. Lovejoy finds it difficult to explain recurrence of similar future-life motifs among widely separated peoples. Notes on white stones causing a living man to go to the land of the dead; dead man carried toward a dead-man country; examples from South American tribes and a Melanesian/Indian-well motif. Right page: Nat. Rev. body; Hewitt material on Cheyenne beliefs in two gods/powers, one good and one bad, with creation and death but no clear moral responsibility or afterlife destiny based on merit.
uncertain_readings: Proper names and abbreviated ethnographic/bibliographic references retained conservatively where handwriting is unclear.

pages.corrected_text: Relation of gods to present life. Lovejoy says the Cheyenne material denies a moral character and shows ritual ideas, while also showing the beginning of access to a happy hunting ground. Entry to heaven may depend on bodily/ritual conditions, including carrying the body or being scalped, rather than ethical merit. Australian reference: belief in happy life in sky; all who die are reunited in future life, with same dress, needs, desires, surroundings, and manner of life.
uncertain_readings: Proper names and abbreviated ethnographic/bibliographic references retained conservatively where handwriting is unclear.

pages.corrected_text: Only an intensified continuation of this world, where only death is eliminated. What is significant is absence of desert: universal happiness for all is a genuinely naturalistic conception. Weak or unhappy worlds can likewise continue earthly conditions without ethical judgment. Right page: one example where an enemy blocks access to a happy hunting ground to prevent a dangerous man from being a danger there; this is practical hostility, not moral judgment. Marginal note cites A. B. Cross, On the Natives of New South Wales, and comparisons with Brahmanism/Buddhism.
uncertain_readings: Proper names and abbreviated ethnographic/bibliographic references retained conservatively where handwriting is unclear.

pages.corrected_text: Belief in relation of spirits to animate human bodies and other objects; spirit as agent making movements. Lovejoy treats some soul conceptions as secondary explanatory devices for physical/mental functions. He argues primitive eschatology contains little moral determination of future life; when moral determination appears it may be a later element. Right page: schematic list of stages/types: separate destinations of dead; special classes of dead; deceased receiving offices/positions; supernatural distinctions not necessarily moral; spirits of dead persons living mostly in same manner as upon earth.
uncertain_readings: Proper names and abbreviated ethnographic/bibliographic references retained conservatively where handwriting is unclear.

pages.corrected_text: Continuation of classification. I: souls in an abode of the dead are those dying of normal causes and continue terrestrial occupations; destiny is a second life. II: certain spirits receive special status/offices, but not on moral considerations. III: a more clearly distinguished celestial/heavenly place develops, with gods/spirits and moral distinctions beginning to appear. Right page: this second plane is invented as machinery to serve an end, moving beyond purely moral grounds toward a preliminary place of trial; souls are judged according to moral behavior during earthly life. Mukkaals/Muckballs [?] or a lord/king of the dead remains a naturalistic being, formerly author of death.
uncertain_readings: Proper names and abbreviated ethnographic/bibliographic references retained conservatively where handwriting is unclear.

pages.corrected_text: The author of death and invention of a personal soul: Lovejoy suggests a possible evolutionary sequence from animism, with many souls in each individual, toward a single reasonable soul residing in the head and dominating other functions. Notes on Todes/Briggs, Primitive Races/Tribes [?], and Marshall. Right page: defined idea of hell, but hell may be a place for those excluded for non-moral reasons. Journey to land of the dead includes river/bridge/thread obstacles and trials; heaven may consist in continuation of ordinary satisfactions. Lovejoy emphasizes these motifs can precede ethical eschatology.
uncertain_readings: Proper names and abbreviated ethnographic/bibliographic references retained conservatively where handwriting is unclear.

pages.corrected_text: Continuation of non-moral trials on journey to land of dead: river, bridge/thread, assistance by antecedent dead or friends in other world. Such eschatology may later be corrupted/reshaped by introduction of ethical ideas. Right page dated May 29: ‘Collect of Religion’ / ‘Relig. & Future’ [?]. Lovejoy states that death itself may be treated as sign of worth/fault but is not a reliable moral selection. Ideas of survival of soul and immortality of gods/spirits may coexist without implying moral immortality; work on this point is noted as incomplete.
uncertain_readings: Proper names and abbreviated ethnographic/bibliographic references retained conservatively where handwriting is unclear.

pages.corrected_text: Continuation of May 29 note. Among many non-European tribes Lovejoy finds clear evidence of influence of Hindu beliefs upon eschatology; yet practices remain inconsistent and the borrowed/moralized eschatology may coexist with animistic-naturalistic and non-moral ideas. Example: a god placed in a favorable position for worship, but afterlife happiness may still consist simply in receiving food and physical satisfactions; descent to a deity’s paradise can mean access to an abode rather than ethical reward.
uncertain_readings: Proper names and abbreviated ethnographic/bibliographic references retained conservatively where handwriting is unclear.

pages.corrected_text:
Same underlying page as p. 28 with a physically inserted slip headed ‘Marillier — Survivance — 12 June’.

Slip: ‘Madagascar: 3 distinct pops. of Madag.’ Lovejoy then distinguishes: (1) ‘The ancient basis’ of the island, whose origin is not known well enough to call it autochthonous; (2) immigrations at an early date from the mainland & Mozambique, with black-slave population noted; (3) ‘The Hovas of F. plateau’, said to belong much more to Asia in their origin than to Africa. He then qualifies the description of Madagascar simply as an African island and records bibliography including Sibree and Le P. Vassière, ‘20 Ans à Madag.’ [Several linking words and one source name remain uncertain.]

pages.corrected_text:
Continuation on physically inserted Marillier survivance sheets. Left slip: the dead are ‘often a grotesque & horrible creature, a sort of animated skeleton’; Lovejoy notes terminology used by one of the non-Hova tribes and then describes an elevated/forest-clad place in or east of Hova country associated with the dead, with an inaccessible or narrow natural passage [place-name and several geographic words uncertain].

Right slip is headed ‘F. occupations of dead or Anthropomorphism.’ It develops a more subtle conception of the soul as a corporeal double of the body which separates from the body at death; it can later undergo a ‘second death’ or annihilation. Lovejoy stresses that the future life may be limited: the soul continues an inferior, bodily-like mode of life for a time rather than possessing necessary immortality. References to Hova language/terms and source pages remain partly compressed.
